War
WAWR
n. (rendering Hebrew milchāmâh and Greek polemos)
From Old North French werre, from a Germanic root meaning confusion or strife — the Romance languages took the word from the Franks because Latin's own bellum died out in the vernacular. The Hebrew milchāmâh comes from lācham, to fight, a verb that also means to eat or devour, so that in Hebrew war is named as a consuming. The English keeps the note of confusion; the Hebrew keeps the note of appetite.

Biblical Definition

Scripture neither romanticises war nor pretends it can be abolished before Christ returns. The Preacher lists it among the appointed seasons of a fallen world — “a time of war, and a time of peace” (Ecc 3:8) — and James traces its origin inward: from whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? War is therefore a symptom of the fall, not an accident of policy. Yet the LORD Himself takes the title: “The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name” (Exo 15:3), sung at the Red Sea when He had fought for a people who held their peace. He is not embarrassed by the name, and He teaches His servants to use the sword when He appoints it — “Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight” (Psa 144:1). At the same time the decisive warfare of the church is of another kind altogether: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4), and the strong holds named are imaginations and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God. The Christian therefore holds two things at once: the magistrate bears the sword, and beareth it not in vain, as God's minister for the punishment of evildoers; and the church advances by the word, by prayer, and by suffering, never by the sword. The end of war is promised but not by human achievement — they shall beat their swords into plowshares when the LORD judges among the nations.

Webster 1828 Definition

Open armed conflict between nations or parties; in Scripture a consequence of the fall traced by James to inward lust, a season appointed under providence, a title the LORD takes as the deliverer of His people, and something wholly distinct from the church's warfare, whose weapons are not carnal.

expand to see more

WAR, n. 1. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs.

2. In Scripture, the LORD is called a man of war, as the deliverer of his people and the avenger of their enemies. Exod. 15.

3. Enmity; state of opposition. The carnal mind is enmity against God; and the flesh lusteth against the spirit.

4. Spiritual warfare; the Christian's conflict with the world, the flesh, and the devil, carried on with weapons that are not carnal. 2 Cor. 10; Eph. 6.

5. To make war; to invade. To be at war; to be in a state of hostility. Man of war; a ship of the line, and in Scripture a warrior.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 3:8 — "A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace."

Exodus 15:3 — "The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name."

2 Corinthians 10:4 — "(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)"

Psalm 144:1 — "A Psalm of David. Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight:"

Modern Corruption

Two errors divide the ground: a pacifism that reads the Sermon on the Mount as abolishing the magistrate's sword, and a militarism that baptises a nation's wars as the LORD's — both collapsing the distinction Scripture keeps between the church and the civil sphere.

expand to see more

The pacifist reading takes resist not evil and turn the other cheek as a rule for magistrates as well as for private men. But the same apostolic writing that forbids the Christian to avenge himself — dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves — immediately grounds the prohibition in the fact that God has appointed someone else to do it: the magistrate is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil, and beareth not the sword in vain. Private vengeance is forbidden precisely because public justice is ordained. John the Baptist did not tell the soldiers to leave their calling but to do violence to no man and be content with their wages, and Cornelius the centurion is commended without any hint that his office was sin.

The opposite error is far more flattering to a nation and therefore more dangerous to a church. Where a country's wars are treated as holy wars, the conquest narratives of Joshua are misapplied to modern states, and the language of Zion is transferred to a flag. Israel's wars of conquest were a unique, commanded, and bounded judgment on the iniquity of the Amorites, executed by a nation under a theocratic covenant that has no successor state. No modern nation stands where Israel stood. The classical Christian answer — that a war may be just when it is declared by lawful authority, for a just cause, with right intention, as a last resort, and waged with restraint toward the innocent — is a discipline of restraint, not a license, and it remains the wiser path between the two errors.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew milchāmâh, from lācham (to fight, also to devour), names war as a consuming; tsābā' is the host or army, whence LORD of hosts. Greek polemos is war and strateia the campaign or warfare, the word of 2Co 10:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew milchāmâh (H4421) — war, battle; some 319 occurrences, from the wars of the LORD to the day of battle.

Hebrew lācham (H3898) — to fight, to do battle; the same consonants also bear the sense to eat, and lechem is bread — war as a devouring.

Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — an army, a host, warfare; the word in the divine title the LORD of hosts, some 285 occurrences.

Greek polemos (G4171) — war, battle; used of wars and rumours of wars (Mat 24:6) and of the war in heaven (Rev 12:7).

Greek strateia (G4752) — a military campaign, warfare; used in 2Co 10:4 of the weapons of our warfare and in 1Ti 1:18 of warring a good warfare.

Usage

"Of appointed seasons and their origin: a time of war, and a time of peace (Ecc 3:8); from whence come wars and fightings among you? (Jas 4:1)."

"Of the LORD as warrior for His people: the LORD is a man of war (Exo 15:3); the LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace (Exo 14:14)."

"Of the church's different warfare: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal (2Co 10:4); we wrestle not against flesh and blood (Eph 6:12)."
